raw_case_text:
In October 2022, a 60-year-old man presented with a two-week history of pruritus, erythema and tender blisters on his body. Before admission, he had been treated with intravenous steroids and antihistamines once for suspected acute urticaria. However, symptoms worsened over the following days. The patient had a history of HIV-1 CDC A2 (classification system according to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention) infection, which had been diagnosed in 2004 and was well controlled with antiretroviral triple therapy (bictegravir 50 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg and tenofovir alafenamide 25 mg) once daily. Viral load was <20 copies/mL and CD4+ count was 418/muL. He had received a third dose of an mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccine in July 2022 and reported no prior history of COVID-19 infection.
At physical examination, multiple blisters ranging in size from millimeters to several centimeters and crusted lesions on erythematous skin were found on his whole body with accentuation on his thighs and upper body ( Figure 1A ). Differential blood count revealed 11% (Ref. 2-4%) of eosinophilic granulocytes (1716/muL total). Total IgE level was 810 kU/L (Ref. <200 kU/L). However, the patient did not have a history of atopic dermatitis, asthma or chronic rhinitis. Highly elevated serum levels of anti-BP180 autoantibodies (147.7 U/mL, Ref. 0-9 U/mL) and linear IgG, IgM and C3 deposits at the dermal-epidermal junction (DEJ) confirmed the diagnosis of BP. For induction therapy, topical mometasone twice daily and oral therapy with prednisolone 80 mg (1 mg/kg body weight) once daily were administered. Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily was added to the initial therapy regimen and switched to dapsone up to 150 mg once daily after 7 days. After two weeks, the patient achieved partial remission, but still developed new lesions with blistering, so he additionally received a total of 160 g (2 g/kg body weight) of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) over 4 days. During the following days no new blisters appeared and he was discharged from hospital after 18 days of treatment. Three weeks later the patient presented with a new flare of pruritic skin erosions and blistering ( Figure 1B ). At this time oral prednisolone was tapered (10-20 mg per week) to a dose of 30 mg once daily. Hence, dupilumab 600 mg was administered subcutaneously for induction and followed by 300 mg every two weeks for maintenance. Also, the dose of oral prednisolone was increased up to 80mg (1 mg/kg body weight) per day. He continued with dapsone 150 mg once daily and oral prednisolone was again tapered over the following weeks (10 mg per week) and then stopped completely due to significant improvement of the skin. At the 2-month follow-up visit in January 2023, the patient reported major relief with no new pruritic lesions or blistering ( Figure 1C ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old man presented in October 2022 with a 2-week history of generalized pruritus, erythema, and tender cutaneous blisters.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks prior to admission, the patient developed widespread pruritus, erythema, and tender bullae over his body. Prior to admission, he received a single course of intravenous corticosteroids and antihistamines for suspected acute urticaria, but his blistering skin lesions progressively worsened.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of HIV-1 infection (CDC Stage A2) diagnosed in 2004, well controlled on once-daily triple antiretroviral therapy. Received a third dose of an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine in July 2022; no prior history of COVID-19 infection, atopic dermatitis, asthma, or chronic rhinitis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe generalized pruritus and tender skin blistering. Home medications: bictegravir 50 mg / emtricitabine 200 mg / tenofovir alafenamide 25 mg once daily.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed multiple tense blisters ranging from millimeters to several centimeters in diameter and crusted erosions on an erythematous base distributed over the entire body, most pronounced on the thighs and upper trunk.
objective.routine_investigations: Differential blood count showed eosinophilia of 11% (1,716/µL total; reference 2–4%). Total serum IgE was elevated at 810 kU/L (reference <200 kU/L). Serum anti-BP180 autoantibodies were markedly elevated at 147.7 U/mL (reference 0–9 U/mL).
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 418 cells/µL. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) / skin immunopathology demonstrated linear deposits of IgG, IgM, and C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) in a 60-year-old man with virologically suppressed HIV-1 infection (plasma HIV-1 viral load <20 copies/mL, CD4+ count 418/µL on bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide), confirmed by elevated anti-BP180 autoantibodies (147.7 U/mL) and linear IgG, IgM, and C3 deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction. Induction therapy included topical mometasone twice daily, oral prednisolone 80 mg/day (1 mg/kg), and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily switched after 7 days to oral dapsone up to 150 mg/day, plus adjuvant intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 160 g [2 g/kg] over 4 days) at week 2 for persistent blistering, allowing hospital discharge on day 18. When a disease flare occurred 3 weeks later during prednisolone taper (at 30 mg/day), subcutaneous dupilumab (600 mg loading dose, then 300 mg every 2 weeks) was initiated alongside temporary re-escalation of prednisolone to 80 mg/day and continued dapsone 150 mg/day. Prednisolone was subsequently tapered off completely, and at the 2-month follow-up in January 2023 the patient remained in complete clinical remission without pruritus or new blisters.
